editorialHook: Three separate stories this week all point to the same conclusion — and it's not what you'd expect.

deepDive.title: The Pattern Nobody's Talking About: AI Adoption Is a Resource Equity Issue
deepDive.summary: This week we covered Boise State's cost-cutting AI platform, OpenAI's HBCU partnership, and Austin CC's free AI literacy certificate. On the surface, three different stories. But here's the pattern: all three are about making AI accessible to populations that would otherwise be left behind. The schools getting ahead aren't the ones with the biggest budgets — they're the ones solving the access problem first.

quickHits.title: Microsoft Copilot Gets Higher Ed-Specific Features
quickHits.summary: Microsoft announced Copilot features designed for higher ed: syllabus generation, assignment scaffolding, and institutional policy awareness. Requires Microsoft 365 Education license.

quickHits.title: First AI-Generated Textbook Approved for State Adoption
quickHits.summary: California approved an AI-generated introductory statistics textbook for state college adoption. The publisher used GPT-4 for initial drafts with human expert review. Cost: $0 for students. This is either the future of OER or a cautionary tale — time will tell.

storiesWatching.label: The Faculty AI Training Gap
storiesWatching.update: A provost at a mid-size public university responded to Tuesday's coverage with a commitment to fund AI training. One down, many to go.

storiesWatching.label: Boise State's Campus-Wide AI Platform
storiesWatching.update: Hearing informal reports that University of Oregon is exploring a similar model. Nothing confirmed yet.

closingThought: Thursday is for stepping back and seeing what the week's stories are really about. This week, that answer is clear: the AI divide in higher ed isn't about technology — it's about access and equity. The institutions that solve for that will define the next decade of education.
